🔍 Google just put an AI chip in orbit

Google’s first orbital AI-chip experiment is now in space and the company says it has established contact and the system is operating as expected.

Launched October 1 aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 Transporter-18, the prototype carries four Trillium TPUs and is running Gemini inference in roughly 15-minute bursts. It then shuts down so its radiators can dump the accumulated heat into space.

The experiment is testing a very different kind of AI infrastructure. There are no fans or air cooling: heat travels through thermal materials and heat pipes before being radiated into space. The satellite also has to deal with radiation, where Google’s testing found the HBM memory was more vulnerable than the TPU itself.

And this is only the beginning. Google plans two more satellites in 2027 to test high-bandwidth laser links between spacecraft, with a longer-term vision of tightly packed orbital clusters containing dozens of TPUs per satellite.

One research concept models an 81-satellite cluster within roughly a 1-km radius, while the broader program has discussed eventually scaling to around 10,000 satellites for a 1 GW orbital AI cluster.

🤔 Could AI become a threat to democracy without taking anyone’s job?

Nobel Prize–winning economist Daron Acemoglu argues that one of AI’s most underestimated consequences may not be mass unemployment, but the concentration of economic power.

AI is making intelligence cheaper and more accessible. But the infrastructure behind it, the most capable models, chips, data, computing capacity and capital remains concentrated among a small number of companies. If AI becomes a major factor of production, those companies could capture an increasingly large share of the value created by the economy.

And economic power can translate into political power.

The same dynamic could play out between countries. The US and China control significant parts of their AI infrastructure, while other countries could see productivity and GDP rise while becoming increasingly dependent on foreign models, chips and computing infrastructure. They may become richer while simultaneously losing some control over the technology driving that growth.

Acemoglu sees a similar risk at every level: individuals may become more productive while losing expertise, companies may become more efficient while losing their competitive advantage, and countries may grow economically while becoming more dependent on external AI infrastructure.

That leads to a much bigger question: if AI concentrates intelligence, capital and infrastructure in fewer hands, can democratic institutions adapt to that concentration of power?

What if AI stopped answering with text? 🤔

Andrej Karpathy thinks the future of AI interfaces could look a lot less like ChatGPT and a lot more like a teacher building something specifically for you.

For simple questions, AI could explain things using ASD-STE100-style simplified English: short sentences, clear words, and as little ambiguity as possible. But when a topic gets complicated, a wall of text may simply be the wrong interface.

Instead, AI could generate a diagram, build a custom interactive webpage, or even create a personal teaching video on the spot, complete with animations inspired by 3Blue1Brown and a synthetic voice.

As AI makes coding and content creation dramatically cheaper, generating a temporary interactive lesson for one person and one question starts to make sense.

🍏 Apple May Break Its September Cycle

According to Bloomberg, new CEO John Ternus wants Apple to release products more often than at its major autumn and spring presentations. He says faster launches and more experiments are needed to stay competitive in the AI era.

Ternus is also considering fewer management layers between engineers and top executives. Over the past 2 weeks, the hardware development team has shed some engineering program managers. Bloomberg reported earlier cuts in the Siri and Vision Pro teams in August.

The rumored pipeline includes a new HomePod mini and iPad mini. Apple is also reportedly working on a new Apple TV 4K, camera-equipped AirPods, touchscreen MacBooks, plus a special iPhone for its 20th anniversary.

🤖 Anthropic Adds Robots to the AI Risk Map

Anthropic estimates that robots can already perform 74% of physical work tasks in the US under at least some conditions. With LLMs added, the figure reaches 81% of all work.

The most exposed roles are mostly vehicle operators. Waste sorting is another example. Waymo robotaxis and autonomous tractors show how the shift works. Sorting robots target recycling work.

With LLMs alone, transport and moving work had under 15% exposure. Robots raise it to about 90%. But exposure means technology can perform part of a job. Robots are currently cost-competitive with humans in only 0.3% of tasks.

📹 HeyGen launches its first video model

The model generates clips from text, animates an image, or uses another video as a reference for motion and visual style. Audio is created with the video, including speech, background sound, and effects.

It runs on MiniMax H3, with additional training by HeyGen. Clips run from 5 to 15 seconds in 480p or 768p, with aspect ratios from 21:9 to 9:16.

HeyGen’s blind comparison put the model first against 4 others, based on 4,800 votes. 768p generation costs $0.03 per second, with a 50% discount through the end of October. It is available through API, OpenRouter, Runware, and ComfyUI. The web version will come later.

🍟 McDonald’s AI Suggests Local Big Mac Prices

In Fresno, a Big Mac costs $5.69 at one McDonald’s and $6.89 at another 2 miles away. That is a 21% gap, linked by Reuters to the chain’s AI pricing system.

The system seeks an “optimal price” for each US restaurant and some overseas markets, based on local customers’ willingness to pay. Franchisees see prompts about price sensitivity. McDonald’s tracks deviations and sends suggestions at least 3 times a year.

Owners formally set the price, but some told Reuters that deviations can trigger calls from headquarters. New franchise standards require them to “constructively engage” with approved pricing tools.

🤖 ChatGPT Gets Virtual Try-On

OpenAI added virtual try-on to ChatGPT. When a clothing product card appears, tap “Try on” and upload a selfie plus a full-body photo. ChatGPT Images 2.5 generates the result.

The feature can also use clothing screenshots, not just items suggested by the bot. Favorite pieces can be saved to Library. Google added the same feature to Search in 2025.

The catch is privacy. By default, images uploaded from a personal account may be used to train models unless you opt out. That includes full-body photos.

🍏 Apple’s Camera Will Not Record Video

Apple is reportedly developing J450, a small cylindrical home security camera with a very low frame rate. AI analyzes what its sensor sees and produces only text descriptions, such as someone entering a room. Face recognition is also expected.

J450 is designed as a companion to Apple’s J490 smart home display. It is part of a broader smart home ecosystem that may include Apple’s own hub, plus security devices from Apple and third parties. Its technology is reportedly similar to what Apple is developing for camera-equipped AirPods.

There will be no video archive to watch later. No video leaves less to leak, while also leaving nothing to review when something happens at home.

🤖 Karpathy Wants AI to Stop Writing Text

Karpathy suggests asking AI to explain complex topics in ASD-STE100 simplified English, with short sentences and little ambiguity. For harder subjects, a diagram or a custom HTML page can work better than plain text.

Modern models can already build one-off interfaces for a specific question. Karpathy is especially interested in personal teaching videos, with animation, a 3Blue1Brown-style explanation, and voice from ElevenLabs or local TTS.

As code and AI work become cheaper, temporary interactive artifacts become practical. The next AI interface may be an answer assembled for each task, rather than an endless chat with walls of text.

🔗 AI Progress Could Compress Years

A Cambridge paper by 22 authors, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, OpenAI’s Jakub Pachocki, and Anthropic’s Jack Clark, examines compressing years of AI progress into months.

At Anthropic, model-written code rose from single digits to over 80% since early 2025. Autonomous R&D tasks rose from 1% to 26% in 6 months. Full automation could make progress 10x faster in about 1.5 years.

Compute or data could limit the scenario. Risks include lost control and a winner gaining too much advantage. The authors propose reporting R&D automation, external audits before deployment, and ways to pause specific data-center workloads.

🇰🇷 South Korea is betting $900B on the AI race

South Korea is planning more than $900 billion in AI-era investment, spanning data centers, semiconductors, HBM memory and physical AI. Samsung and SK alone have announced hundreds of billions of dollars in chip investment, while massive new data-center capacity is being planned through 2035.

Seoul’s wants to turn Korea into a global AI superpower by controlling more of the stack, from the chips powering AI, to the compute running it, to robots and factories using it.

The government has even put “physical AI” alongside semiconductors and AI data centers as pillars of its strategy, linking the AI “brain” to robots and machines operating in the real world.

So this isn’t really $900B being spent on “superintelligence.” It’s a bet that the countries controlling the infrastructure around AI could become just as important as the companies building the models.

And South Korea clearly wants to be one of them.

⚠️ AI consciousness may finally be testable

For decades, AI consciousness was mostly a philosophical debate. There was no clear way to test whether a machine was actually experiencing anything.

Now researchers have proposed MEM, Motivated Emotional Mind, a mathematical and architectural framework designed to make machine consciousness a falsifiable hypothesis.

The framework argues that language fluency, multimodality, memory, planning or even a humanoid body aren’t enough to establish consciousness.

Instead, researchers should look for specific architectural and causal properties that can be experimentally tested and potentially disproven.

That could become crucial as AI systems become increasingly convincing and millions of people form emotional relationships with them.

We may soon have to answer a strange question: is there actually a mind behind the machine, or are we simply watching an incredibly convincing simulation?

🥺 Sam Altman says OpenAI is willing to let some things go wrong

Sam Altman is offering an unusually blunt look at how OpenAI is thinking about AI risk and the trade-offs are becoming harder to hide.

Altman says OpenAI is willing to accept “some things going wrong” rather than allow enormous AI capabilities to become concentrated in a handful of companies, people or countries. He specifically points to open-source models, while warning that they could trigger “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems.”

On President Trump’s new AI accord, Altman says it currently has “no real power” and argues that more governance will eventually be needed. His dividing line is clear: ordinary failures can be tolerated, but losing meaningful human control over AI cannot.

That philosophy also puts an enormous amount of judgment on OpenAI itself. Altman admits: “I’m going to make many individual decisions that you’re clearly not going to like.”

His response to critics? “Come try making them all; they’re not so easy.”

And OpenAI is already making those calls. Altman says Astra 6.1 was “ready to go,” but the version they had prepared would have “tipped too much towards the accident risk.” OpenAI therefore delayed it, choosing to work toward a version it believes can be distributed more broadly with greater confidence in its alignment.

❗️AI could make you guilty on video

Sundar Pichai warned about a disturbing possibility: someone could use AI to create a convincing video of you saying something you never said.

Your face. Your voice. A fake confession.

Then they send it to your boss, your family or your friends and demand money to make it disappear.

We’ve already seen scammers use fake versions of famous people to push crypto scams. Now imagine that same technology being used against an ordinary person.

You say the video is fake.

They say you’re lying.

And everyone watching has “proof.”

The terrifying part isn’t that AI wants to frame you. It’s that someone else can use your identity as a weapon.

If seeing is no longer believing, how do you prove you didn’t do something that never happened?

🤖 ChatGPT may start changing how it writes in the EU

OpenAI is reportedly preparing invisible text watermarks for ChatGPT and Codex outputs in the EU, with the pattern embedded directly into the wording.

The reason is the EU AI Act, which is pushing AI-generated content toward being identifiable.

OpenAI says its testing found no meaningful impact on quality. But there’s a bigger issue: detection requirements could start influencing how an AI actually phrases your text.

And the watermark isn’t particularly robust.

In one test using 400-token passages, changing just 25% of the words to synonyms reportedly reduced detection from around 92% to 17%.

There’s another problem:m, it can’t tell how much of the text came from a human.

You could write something yourself, ask ChatGPT to edit it, and the final version could still carry the watermark.

📢 Your voice could become a trademark

Law firms may soon be selling “identity portfolios” that protect a person’s face, voice and signature phrases, much like companies protect their brands.

Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has just taken a step in that direction. She filed an application with the EU Intellectual Property Office to register her voice as a sound mark, using a four-second recording of herself saying “Io sono Giorgia Meloni.” The application is still under examination.

The goal is to give her another legal tool against AI-generated voice clones and deepfakes. Meloni has already been targeted by manipulated content, including fake material and misleading uses of her voice.

If this approach catches on, protecting your identity could start looking a lot like protecting a corporate brand.

Your face. Your voice. Your catchphrases.

All potentially becoming intellectual property in the fight against AI impersonation.

❗️AI hits biology’s data bottleneck

AI biology has reached a problem GPUs alone can’t solve: there simply isn’t enough training data.

A $1.8 billion effort backed by Biohub, the U.S. Department of Energy, NIH, Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs aims to build a “universal virtual cell” that could predict how cells respond to interventions and let researchers test biological experiments digitally before doing them in the lab.

Today’s datasets contain hundreds of millions of cells. Future models may need billions and eventually trillions. The goal is to compress work that normally takes decades into about five years, with the first dataset expected in roughly one year.

There’s also an unusual access model: commercial funders get one year of exclusive access to the data they help generate before it becomes public. Government-funded data has no such embargo.

❗️Hacker may have exposed himself by asking AI to write his résumé

A hacker suspected of targeting South Korean banks may have accidentally revealed his identity after asking Claude Code to write a résumé about his own hacking activities.

CrowdStrike traced the attacks to infrastructure running an AI hacking tool called ARTEX. Investigators later found publicly exposed folders containing the attacker’s saved Claude Code conversations.

In one chat, he asked Claude to create a cybersecurity résumé describing his ARTEX work and provided personal details including a phone number, Telegram handle, claimed age of 26, university and location in China. The same Telegram handle appeared in other hacking-related conversations.

He had also asked Claude where stolen Korean data is typically sold.

His identity has not been independently confirmed but asking an AI to turn your own cybercrime history into a résumé is certainly an unusual way to leave a trail.

💰 AI agents are becoming major users of economic data

AI agents now account for roughly half of all visits to FRED, the St. Louis Fed’s economic data portal, according to Bloomberg.

That changes what a data platform like FRED needs to be designed for. Humans see a chart alongside its source, notes and footnotes. An AI agent can simply extract the numbers, interpret them and rebuild them into an answer, potentially leaving important context and provenance behind.

As more AI systems become the middleman between people and economic data, making sure they preserve where numbers came from could become just as important as the numbers themselves.

❗️AI is starting to trigger a backlash in mathematics

OpenAI’s release of 722 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts is already causing a backlash among some mathematicians.

The Association for Human Mathematics (AHM) criticized the release and urged mathematicians to “discontinue their work with OpenAI.” Terence Tao also reposted the AHM statement on his blog.

The debate is bigger than whether AI-generated proofs are good or bad. If AI can increasingly produce serious mathematical results, the field now has to figure out how to verify, publish and evaluate them.

Walking away from the technology doesn’t resolve that question. The more interesting challenge is figuring out how mathematicians and AI can actually work together.

❗️The AI domain war has officially begun

OpenAI, Google and Meta are now fighting over some of the most valuable AI-related internet domains.

ICANN received 1,615 applications from 481 applicants in its first new domain expansion since 2012. OpenAI applied for 15 domains, including .agent, .agi, .asi, .chatgpt, .gpt, .mcp, .model and .openai.

Google went even bigger with 39 applications, including .agent, .mcp, .gemini, .deepmind and .api. Meta submitted 18, including .agent, .llama, .metaai and .superintelligence.

Some strings are already crowded: .agent has 13 applicants, .agi has 7, and .mcp has 5. Interestingly, Anthropic, which created MCP didn’t apply for .mcp at all.

Anthropic only applied for .anthropic and .claude, while Microsoft went for .copilot and .msft.

Each application costs $227,000, and contested domains can become extremely expensive. Google previously paid $25 million for .app.

The process could continue until 2030, and none of these domains has been awarded yet.
